consumer_seed: The Ofcom broadband-speeds guide was published on 21 November 2022.
The Broadband Speeds Code of Practice requires clear speed information when a broadband service is bought.
For a provider-network speed problem that cannot be fixed within 30 days, a covered customer must be allowed to leave without an early exit fee.
BT is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
EE is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
NOW Broadband is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
Plusnet is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
Sky is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
TalkTalk is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
Utility Warehouse is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
Virgin Media is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
Zen Internet is listed among providers covered by the broadband-speed protections.
A customer should receive accurate information about expected broadband speed without having to ask for it.
The guide defines the busy-time estimate window for home broadband as 8pm to 10pm.
The guide defines the busy-time estimate window for business broadband as noon to 2pm.
A covered provider should give the customer a personalised minimum guaranteed broadband speed.
For superfast products, the minimum-speed information is based on the capability of the line entering the home or office.
An Ethernet-connected computer or tablet gives a more accurate speed test than Wi-Fi, which can slow the signal.
A customer can check the contract or ask the provider to determine the speed that should be delivered.
The right to exit for an unresolved covered speed problem also applies to financially, contractually or technically linked bundled products.
The code's 30-day process does not apply to rolling monthly contracts, which can usually be left by giving notice.
After purchase, the provider should send speed estimates, relevant speed-policy details and instructions for problems below the guarantee.
A delayed service start or missed engineer appointment can fall under Ofcom's automatic-compensation scheme.
Broadband advertisements must show the average speed received by at least 50% of customers at the network's busiest time.
The Ofcom social-tariff page was published on 6 March 2024.
The Ofcom social-tariff page was last updated on 22 June 2026.
Social tariffs are lower-priced broadband or phone packages for people receiving specified benefits.
A household receiving Universal Credit can qualify for the listed social tariffs.
The page states that current social-tariff prices range from £10 to £24.
Most listed social tariffs provide unlimited broadband at speeds above 30 Mbit/s.
Where setup charges apply, Ofcom says they should be small and disclosed before sign-up.
A customer can switch to a social tariff offered by the current provider at any time without a switching charge.
The agreed social-tariff price should not increase during the contract.
A customer should not pay an early-exit fee to leave a social tariff.
BT and KCOM also provide cheaper voice-only landline tariffs to eligible households.
Major providers include Pension Credit, Employment and Support Allowance, Jobseeker's Allowance and Income Support among qualifying benefits.
Some providers also include benefits such as Personal Independence Payment and Attendance Allowance.
The person receiving the qualifying benefit must be the main person named on the contract.
Most social tariffs can be applied for online or by calling the provider.
A customer whose current provider has no social tariff can switch to a provider that offers one.
A provider may allow a customer to leave an existing contract without a penalty to move to a social tariff elsewhere.
The listed 4th Utility Social Tariff costs £13.99 per month and advertises 30 Mbit/s in England.
The listed BT Home Essentials Unlimited 36 package costs £21 per month and advertises 36 Mbit/s across the UK.
The listed Community Fibre Essential package costs £12.50 per month and advertises 35 Mbit/s in London.
The Ofcom broadband universal-service guide was published on 8 August 2023.
The guide was last updated on 20 March 2026.
Every UK home and business has a legal right to request a decent and affordable broadband connection.
A decent connection is defined as providing at least 10 Mbit/s download speed.
A decent connection is defined as providing at least 1 Mbit/s upload speed.
Eligible premises outside Hull can request an upgraded universal-service connection from BT.
Eligible premises in the Hull area can request an upgraded universal-service connection from KCOM.
An applicant does not need to be an existing BT or KCOM customer.
BT or KCOM has 30 days after contact to confirm eligibility and the likely build cost.
Eligibility requires that the home or business has no access to an existing decent broadband service.
Eligibility also requires that no public broadband scheme is expected to cover the premises in the next 12 months.
A premises with only a decent service priced above £59.60 per month can also request a universal-service connection.
If the applicant's share of build or upgrade cost is £3,400 or less, the applicant does not pay for that work.
Where the connection cost exceeds £3,400, an applicant choosing to proceed must pay the excess.
For an excess-cost connection, BT or KCOM will conduct a survey and provide a quote within 60 days.
The new broadband service must be priced no higher than £59.60 per month.
Most eligible connections should be delivered within 12 months.
Some eligible universal-service connections can take up to 24 months.
A person who is not eligible may be offered satellite broadband as an alternative option.
BT or KCOM should explain the right to challenge an ineligibility decision and how to complain.
The Ofcom ADR guide was published on 8 March 2024.
The Ofcom ADR guide was last updated on 20 July 2026.
The first complaint step is to contact the provider's customer-services department.
If customer service does not resolve the problem, the customer should make a formal complaint to the provider.
An eligible unresolved complaint can be taken to an ADR scheme free of charge.
ADR schemes are independent bodies that impartially assess complaints against phone or broadband providers.
Residential customers are within the listed ADR eligibility scope.
A small business with up to 10 employees is within the listed ADR eligibility scope.
A not-for-profit organisation with up to 10 working individuals, excluding volunteers, is within the listed ADR eligibility scope.
The complaint must already have been raised with the provider.
The provider complaint must remain unresolved before the customer uses ADR.
A complaint can be escalated after at least six weeks from the initial complaint.
A complaint can be escalated sooner where agreement has not been reached and the customer has a deadlock letter.
The complaint must be referred to ADR less than 12 months after the deadlock letter.
Phone and broadband companies must maintain an easily accessible complaints code of practice.
The complaints code must include a phone number, postal address and email address or webform.
The complaints code must describe investigation steps and resolution timeframes.
Providers must take prompt and active steps to resolve complaints and promptly communicate outcomes.
Ofcom approves two telecoms ADR schemes: CISAS and Communications Ombudsman.
Customers whose provider is not listed on the Ofcom page can ask the ADR schemes which scheme the provider belongs to.
